question.text: A farmer expects to harvest wheat in 3 months and wants to lock in a minimum selling price. Which option strategy is appropriate?

answer.text: Buy put options on wheat to guarantee a minimum selling price
Buy call options on wheat to benefit from price increases
Sell call options on wheat to earn premium income
Sell put options on wheat to lock in the purchase price

explanation.text: The Logic: The farmer is a future seller of wheat and is exposed to a price fall before harvest. Buying a put option gives the right (but not the obligation) to sell at the strike price, which effectively locks in a minimum selling price (strike less premium paid). If prices fall, the put is exercised at the strike; if prices rise, the put is allowed to lapse and the wheat is sold in the spot market at the higher price, with only the premium foregone. The Trap: Buying calls would benefit a buyer of wheat, not a seller — wrong directional exposure. Selling calls only earns a fixed premium and offers no downside protection. Selling puts obligates the farmer to buy more wheat, which is the opposite of what is needed. Note: The cited NISM-Series-VIII workbook pages (48-49, 70-72, 115, 117, 119-120) frame the farmer hedge example through selling wheat futures rather than buying puts on wheat to lock a minimum selling price. The framing above is general options-hedging theory (long-put protective hedge for a producer) rather than a direct workbook citation.
